{{Short description|Map between simplicial sets with lifting property}}
In mathematics, '''Kan complexes''' and '''Kan fibrations''' are part of the theory of [[simplicial set]]s. Kan fibrations are the fibrations of the standard [[model category]] structure on simplicial sets and are therefore of fundamental importance. Kan complexes are the [[fibrant object]]s in this model category. The name is in honor of [[Daniel Kan]].

For various kinds of fibrations for simplicial sets, see [[Fibration of simplicial sets]].
==Definitions==

=== Definition of the standard n-simplex ===
[[File:2dKanFibration.svg|thumb|right|The striped blue simplex in the domain has to exist in order for this map to be a Kan fibration]]

For each ''n''&nbsp;≥&nbsp;0, recall that the [[Simplicial set#The standard n-simplex and the simplex category|standard <math>n</math>-simplex]], <math>\Delta^n</math>, is the representable simplicial set
:<math>\Delta^n(i) = \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf{\Delta}} ([i], [n])</math>
Applying the [[Simplicial set#Geometric realization|geometric realization]] functor to this simplicial set gives a space homeomorphic to the [[Simplex#The standard simplex|topological standard <math>n</math>-simplex]]: the convex subspace of <math>\mathbb{R}^{n+1}</math> consisting of all points <math>(t_0,\dots,t_n)</math> such that the coordinates are non-negative and sum to 1.

=== Definition of a horn ===
For each ''k''&nbsp;≤&nbsp;''n'', this has a subcomplex <math>\Lambda^n_k</math>, the ''k''-th horn inside <math>\Delta^n</math>, corresponding to the boundary of the ''n''-simplex, with the ''k''-th face removed. This may be formally defined in various ways, as for instance the union of the images of the ''n'' maps <math>\Delta^{n-1} \rightarrow \Delta^n</math> corresponding to all the other faces of <math>\Delta^n</math>.<ref>See Goerss and Jardine, page 7</ref> Horns of the form <math>\Lambda_k^2</math> sitting inside <math>\Delta^2</math> look like the black V at the top of the adjacent image. If <math>X</math> is a simplicial set, then maps
:<math>s: \Lambda_k^n \to X</math>
correspond to collections of <math>n</math> <math>(n-1)</math>-simplices satisfying a compatibility condition, one for each <math>0 \leq k \leq n</math>. Explicitly, this condition can be written as follows. Write the <math>(n-1)</math>-simplices as a list <math>(s_0,\dots,s_{k-1},s_{k+1},\dots,s_{n})</math> and require that
:<math>d_i s_j = d_{j-1} s_i\,</math> for all <math>i < j</math> with <math>i,j \neq k</math>.<ref>{{harvnb|May|1992|page=2}}</ref>

These conditions are satisfied for the <math>(n-1)</math>-simplices of <math>\Lambda_k^n</math> sitting inside <math>\Delta^n</math>.

=== Definition of a Kan fibration ===
[[File:Kan fibration.png|thumb|right|Lifting diagram for a Kan fibration]]
A map of simplicial sets <math>f: X\rightarrow Y</math> is a '''Kan fibration''' if, for any <math>n\ge 1</math> and <math>0\le k\le n</math>, and for any maps <math>s:\Lambda^n_k\rightarrow X</math> and <math>y:\Delta^n\rightarrow Y\,</math> such that <math>f \circ s=y \circ i</math> (where <math>i</math> is the inclusion of <math>\Lambda^n_k</math> in <math>\Delta^n</math>), there exists a map <math>x:\Delta^n \rightarrow X</math> such that <math>s=x \circ i</math> and 
<math>y=f \circ x</math>. Stated this way, the definition is <u>very similar</u> to that of [[fibration]]s in [[topology]] (see also [[homotopy lifting property]]), whence the name "fibration".

==== Technical remarks ====
Using the correspondence between <math>n</math>-simplices of a simplicial set <math>X</math> and morphisms <math>\Delta^n \to X</math> (a consequence of the [[Yoneda lemma]]), this definition can be written in terms of simplices. The image of the map <math>fs: \Lambda_k^n \to Y</math> can be thought of as a horn as described above. Asking that <math>fs</math> factors through <math>yi</math> corresponds to requiring that there is an <math>n</math>-simplex in <math>Y</math> whose faces make up the horn from <math>fs</math> (together with one other face). Then the required map <math>x: \Delta^n\to X</math> corresponds to a simplex in <math>X</math> whose faces include the horn from <math>s</math>. The diagram to the right is an example in two dimensions. Since the black V in the lower diagram is filled in by the blue <math>2</math>-simplex, if the black V above maps down to it then the striped blue <math>2</math>-simplex has to exist, along with the dotted blue <math>1</math>-simplex, mapping down in the obvious way.<ref>May uses this simplicial definition; see {{harvnb|May|1992|page=25}}</ref>

==== Kan complexes defined from Kan fibrations ====
A simplicial set <math>X</math> is called a '''Kan complex''' if the map from <math>X \to \{*\}</math>, the one-point simplicial set, is a Kan fibration. In the [[model category]] for simplicial sets, <math>\{*\}</math> is the [[Initial and terminal objects|terminal object]] and so a Kan complex is exactly the same as a [[fibrant object]]. Equivalently, this could be stated as: if every map <math>\alpha: \Lambda^n_k \to X</math> from a horn has an extension to <math>\Delta^n</math>, meaning there is a lift <math>\tilde{\alpha}: \Delta^n \to X</math> such that<blockquote><math>\alpha = \tilde{\alpha}\circ \iota</math></blockquote>for the [[inclusion map]] <math>\iota: \Lambda^n_k \hookrightarrow \Delta^n</math>, then <math>X</math> is a Kan complex. Conversely, every Kan complex has this property, hence it gives a simple technical condition for a Kan complex.

==Examples==

=== Simplicial sets from singular homology ===
An important example comes from the construction of [[Singular homology#Singular simplices|singular simplices]] used to define [[singular homology]], called the '''singular functor'''<ref name=":0">{{Cite book|last1=Goerss|first1=Paul G.|title=Simplicial Homotopy Theory|last2=Jardine|first2=John F.|date=2009|publisher=Birkhäuser Basel|isbn=978-3-0346-0188-7|oclc=837507571}}</ref><sup>pg 7</sup><blockquote><math>S: \text{Top} \to s\text{Sets}</math>.</blockquote>Given a space <math>X</math>, define a singular <math>n</math>-simplex of X to be a continuous map from the standard topological <math>n</math>-simplex (as described above) to <math>X</math>,
:<math>f: \Delta_n \to X</math>
Taking the set of these maps for all non-negative <math>n</math> gives a graded set,
:<math>S(X) = \coprod_n S_n(X)</math>.
To make this into a simplicial set, define face maps <math>d_i: S_n(X)\to S_{n-1}(X)</math> by
:<math>(d_i f)(t_0,\dots,t_{n-1}) = f(t_0,\dots,t_{i-1},0,t_i,\dots,t_{n-1})\,</math>
and degeneracy maps <math>s_i: S_n(X)\to S_{n+1}(X)</math> by
:<math>(s_i f)(t_0,\dots,t_{n+1}) = f(t_0,\dots,t_{i-1},t_i + t_{i+1},t_{i+2},\dots,t_{n+1})\,</math>.
Since the union of any <math>n+1</math> faces of <math>\Delta_{n+1}</math> is a strong [[deformation retract]] of <math>\Delta_{n+1}</math>, any [[continuous function]] defined on these faces can be extended to <math>\Delta_{n+1}</math>, which shows that <math>S(X)</math> is a Kan complex.<ref>See May, page 3</ref>

==== Relation with geometric realization ====
It is worth noting the singular functor is [[Adjoint functors|right adjoint]] to the [[geometric realization functor]]<blockquote><math>|\cdot|:s\text{Sets} \to \text{Top}</math></blockquote>giving the isomorphism<blockquote><math>\text{Hom}_{\text{Top}}(|X|,Y) \cong \text{Hom}_{s\text{Sets}}(X,S(Y))</math></blockquote>

See also: [[Milnor's theorem on Kan complexes]].

=== Simplicial sets underlying simplicial groups ===
It can be shown that the simplicial set underlying a [[simplicial group]] is always fibrant<ref name=":0" /><sup>pg 12</sup>. In particular, for a [[simplicial abelian group]], its geometric realization is homotopy equivalent to a product of Eilenberg-Maclane spaces<blockquote><math>\prod_{i \in I} K(A_i,n_i)</math></blockquote>In particular, this includes [[classifying space]]s. So the spaces <math>S^1 \simeq K(\mathbb{Z},1)</math>, <math>\mathbb{CP}^\infty \simeq K(\mathbb{Z},2)</math>, and the infinite lens spaces <math>L^\infty_q \simeq K(\mathbb{Z}/q, 2)</math> are correspond to Kan complexes of some simplicial set. In fact, this set can be constructed explicitly using the [[Dold–Kan correspondence]] of a chain complex and taking the underlying simplicial set of the simplicial abelian group.

=== Geometric realizations of small groupoids ===
Another important source of examples are the simplicial sets associated to a small groupoid <math>\mathcal{G}</math>. This is defined as the geometric realization of the simplicial set <math>[\Delta^{op},\mathcal{G}]</math> and is typically denoted <math>B\mathcal{G}</math>. We could have also replaced <math>\mathcal{G}</math> with an infinity groupoid. It is conjectured that the homotopy category of geometric realizations of infinity groupoids is equivalent to the homotopy category of homotopy types. This is called the [[homotopy hypothesis]].

=== Mapping space ===
Let <math>X</math> be an ∞-category. Then for each object <math>x, y</math>, let <math>\operatorname{Map}_X(x, y)</math> be the fiber of <math>(s, t) : \underline{\operatorname{Hom}}(\Delta^1, X) \to X^2</math> over the point <math>(x, y)</math>. Then <math>\operatorname{Map}_X(x, y)</math> is a Kan complex.<ref>{{harvnb|Cisinski|2023|loc=§ 3.7.1.}}</ref>

=== Postnikov section ===
Let ''X'' be a Kan complex. Then the n''-th Postnikov section'' <math>P_n X</math> is a simplicial set such that <math>P_n X_m</math> is the [[coequalizer]] of <math>X_m \rightrightarrows \operatorname{cosk}_n X_m</math>.<ref>§ 5.6. in {{Cite book| first=John F.|last= Jardine|authorlink=Rick Jardine| title=Local homotopy theory|series= Springer Monographs in Mathematics| publisher=Springer-Verlag|location= New York|year=2015|mr=3309296|doi=10.1007/978-1-4939-2300-7|isbn= 978-1-4939-2299-4}}</ref> Then the following can be verified directly:
*<math>P_n X</math> is a Kan complex and <math>X \to P_nX</math> is a Kan fibration.
*The induced map <math>\pi_i X \to \pi_i P_n X</math> is an isomorphism for <math>i = 0</math> and for each <math>0 < i \le n</math> and choice of a base point on ''X''.
*<math>\pi_i X = 0</math> for each <math>i > n</math> and choice of a base point on ''X''.

For a simplicial set ''X'', we then let <math>P_n X = P_n \operatorname{Ex}^{\infty} X</math> where <math>\operatorname{Ex}^{\infty}</math> is an [[Ex∞ functor]].

=== Non-example: standard n-simplex ===
It turns out the standard <math>n</math>-simplex <math>\Delta^n</math> is not a Kan complex<ref>{{cite arXiv|last=Friedman|first=Greg|date=2016-10-03|title=An elementary illustrated introduction to simplicial sets|class=math.AT|eprint=0809.4221}}</ref><sup>pg 38</sup>. The construction of a counter example in general can be found by looking at a low dimensional example, say <math>\Delta^1</math>. Taking the map <math>\Lambda_0^2 \to \Delta^1</math> sending<blockquote><math>\begin{matrix}
[0,2] \mapsto [0,0] & 
[0,1] \mapsto [0,1]
\end{matrix}</math></blockquote>gives a counter example since it cannot be extended to a map <math>\Delta^2 \to \Delta^1</math> because the maps have to be order preserving. If there was a map, it would have to send<blockquote><math>\begin{align}
0 \mapsto 0 \\
1 \mapsto 1 \\
2 \mapsto 0
\end{align}</math></blockquote>but this isn't a map of simplicial sets.

== Categorical properties ==

=== Simplicial enrichment and function complexes ===
For simplicial sets <math>X,Y</math> there is an associated simplicial set called the '''function complex''' <math>\textbf{Hom}(X,Y)</math>, where the simplices are defined as<blockquote><math>\textbf{Hom}_n(X,Y) = \text{Hom}_{s\text{Sets}}(X\times\Delta^n, Y)</math></blockquote>and for an ordinal map <math>\theta : [m] \to [n]</math> there is an induced map<blockquote><math>\theta^*: \textbf{Hom}(X,Y)_n \to \textbf{Hom}(X,Y)_m</math></blockquote>(since the first factor of Hom is contravariant) defined by sending a map <math>f:X\times\Delta^n \to Y</math> to the composition<blockquote><math>X\times\Delta^m \xrightarrow{1\times \theta}X\times\Delta^n \xrightarrow{f} Y</math></blockquote>

==== Exponential law ====
This complex has the following exponential law of simplicial sets<blockquote>
<math>\text{ev}_*:\text{Hom}_{s\text{Sets}}(K, \textbf{Hom}(X,Y)) \to \text{Hom}_{s\text{Sets}}(X\times K, Y)</math></blockquote>
which sends a map <math>f: K \to \textbf{Hom}(X,Y)</math> to the composite map<blockquote>
<math>X\times K \xrightarrow{1\times g}X\times\textbf{Hom}(X,Y) \xrightarrow{ev} Y</math></blockquote>
where <math>ev(x,f) = f(x,\iota_n)</math> for <math>\iota_n \in \text{Hom}_\Delta([n],[n])</math> lifted to the n-simplex <math>\Delta^n</math>.

=== Kan fibrations and pull-backs ===
Given a (Kan) fibration <math>p:X \to Y</math> and an inclusion of simplicial sets <math>i: K \hookrightarrow L</math>, there is a fibration<ref name=":0" /> <sup>pg 21</sup><blockquote><math>\textbf{Hom}(L,X) \xrightarrow{(i^*,p_*)}\textbf{Hom}(K,X)\times_{\textbf{Hom}(K,Y)}\textbf{Hom}(L, Y)</math></blockquote>(where <math>\textbf{Hom}</math> is in the function complex in the category of simplicial sets) induced from the [[commutative diagram]]<blockquote><math>\begin{matrix}
\textbf{Hom}(L,X) & \xrightarrow{p_*} & \textbf{Hom}(L,Y) \\
i^* \downarrow & & \downarrow i^* \\
\textbf{Hom}(K,X) & \xrightarrow{p_*} & \textbf{Hom}(K,Y)
\end{matrix}</math></blockquote>where <math>i^*</math> is the pull-back map given by pre-composition and <math>p_*</math> is the pushforward map given by post-composition. In particular, the previous fibration implies <math>p_*:\textbf{Hom}(L,X) \to \textbf{Hom}(L,Y)</math> and <math>i^*:\textbf{Hom}(L,Y) \to \textbf{Hom}(K,Y)</math> are fibrations.

The above is a consequence of a [[theorem of Gabriel and Zisman]].

== Homotopy groups of Kan complexes ==
{{main|Simplicial homotopy group}}
The [[homotopy group]]s of a fibrant simplicial set may be defined combinatorially, using horns, in a way that agrees with the homotopy groups of the topological space which realizes it. For a Kan complex <math>X</math> and a vertex <math>x:\Delta^0 \to X</math>, as a set <math>\pi_n(X,x)</math> is defined as the set of maps <math>\alpha:\Delta^n \to X</math> of simplicial sets fitting into a certain commutative diagram: <blockquote><math>\pi_n(X,x) =
\left\{
\alpha: \Delta^n \to X :
\begin{matrix}
\Delta^n & \overset{\alpha}{\to} & X \\
\uparrow & & \uparrow x \\
\partial \Delta^n & \to & \Delta^0
\end{matrix} \right\}</math></blockquote>Notice the fact <math>\partial\Delta^n</math> is mapped to a point is equivalent to the definition of the sphere <math>S^n</math> as the quotient <math>B^n / \partial B^n</math> for the standard unit ball<blockquote><math>B^n = \{x \in \mathbb{R}^n : ||x||_{eu} \leq 1 \}</math></blockquote>Defining the group structure requires a little more work. Essentially, given two maps <math>\alpha,\beta:\Delta^n \to X</math> there is an associated <math>(n+1)</math>-simplice <math>\omega:\Delta^{n+1} \to X</math> such that <math>d_n\omega:\Delta^n \to X</math> gives their addition. This map is well-defined up to simplicial homotopy classes of maps, giving the group structure. Moreover, the groups <math>\pi_n(X,x)</math> are Abelian for <math>n \geq 2</math>. For <math>\pi_0(X)</math>, it is defined as the homotopy classes <math>[x ]</math> of vertex maps <math>x:\Delta^0 \to X</math>.

=== Homotopy groups of simplicial sets ===
Using model categories, any simplicial set <math>X</math> has a fibrant replacement <math>\hat{X}</math> which is homotopy equivalent to <math>X</math> in the homotopy category of simplicial sets. Then, the homotopy groups of <math>X</math> can be defined as{{fact|date=April 2025}}<blockquote><math>\pi_n(X,x) := \pi_n(\hat{X},\hat{x})</math></blockquote>where <math>\hat{x}</math> is a lift of <math>x:\Delta^0 \to X</math> to <math>\hat{X}</math>. These fibrant replacements can be thought of a topological analogue of [[Resolution (algebra)|resolutions of a chain complex]] (such as a [[projective resolution]] or a [[flat resolution]]).

== Kan ==
Kan complexes themselves form a [[weak Kan complex]] called '''Kan'''. Namely, first consider the category ''K'' where objects are Kan complexes and morphisms maps of simplicial sets.  As a category of presheaves has internal Hom, each hom-set in ''K'' has a structure of a simplicial set; in short, ''K'' is a simplicial category. The [[homotopy coherent nerve]] of it
:<math>\textbf{Kan} := N^{hc}(K)</math>
is then a weak Kan complex (∞-category).<ref>{{cite web|url=https://kerodon.net/tag/00TZ|title=Construction 5.5.1.1 (The ∞-Category of Spaces)|work=Keradon: an online resource for homotopy-coherent mathematics|first=Jacob|last=Lurie|author-link=Jacob Lurie}}</ref> In view of [[homotopy hypothesis]], it is often taken as the ∞-category of spaces = ∞-groupoids and is also denoted as <math>\mathsf{S}</math> or some other variants.

See also: [[universal left fibration]].
